newsitem.title: GERMANY: SPD says can't block scrapping German wealth tax.
newsitem.headline: SPD says can't block scrapping German wealth tax.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) conceded on Friday they could no longer block the abolition of wealth taxes, a row over which has held up passage of the government's 1997 tax bill.

Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier, the SPD spokeswoman on finance, told parliament the wealth tax could no longer be raised from the start of next year. But, she added, "We will fight the government's blockade on the wealth tax to the end."

The wealth tax had been ruled illegal by Germany's constitutional court. The SPD, wielding its majority in the upper house of parliament to block the tax bill, had sought to keep the wealth tax on private fortunes.
But the opposition was finally forced to cave after leaders from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition threatened to let the tax bill fail rather than back down.
Speaking earlier, Finance Minister Theo Waigel defended the abolition of the tax, saying it would be offset by increases in inheritance taxes.
"The fact is that with the end of the wealth tax there will be no tax giveaway for the rich," Waigel told deputies, adding that the wealth tax destroyed jobs by eating into the capital of companies.

Waigel's tax bill has gone into parliament's mediation process, and negotiators on Thursday reported progress towards compensating for the resulting shortfall in funding of nine billion marks ($5.87 billion) which would fall on Germany's 16 states.
Talks will continue next Wednesday on drafting a final tax measure which could be put to a vote in the Bundesrat.
The Bundesrat lower house was holding a final debate on the 1997 federal budget, which would cut spending by 2.5 percent to 440 billion marks.

The measure foresees a budget deficit of 2.5 percent of gross domestic product, enabling Germany to meet the Maastricht treaty's deficit target of three percent -- one of the criteria set for qualifying for European monetary union.
Final votes on the budget were imminent.
